newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-EMPTY SEATS CAST DOUBTS ON ATHENS OLYMPIC BID.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-EMPTY SEATS CAST DOUBTS ON ATHENS OLYMPIC BID.

text.p: Empty seats in the Olympic stadium during the sixth world championships here have dealt a blow to Greek prospects of hosting the 2004 Olympics.

"The empty seats don't look good. This is a marvelous stadium and it should have been packed for such event which is also supposed to promote the Athens 2004 bid," a member of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) told Reuters.
"I am sure that if this continues it will be taken into account when the IOC votes for the venue of the 2004 Games next month."

The championships are being scrutinised by some 40 visiting IOC members and despite assurances by the organisers that 75 percent of the tickets were sold, the 60,000-seat stadium is half full even for flagship events such as Sunday's 100 metres finals.

"I am really sorry that the stadium is not full. Athens is bidding for the Olympics and the people of Athens look down on such a great event," said Greek high jump champion Lambros Papakostas who qualified for Wednesday's finals.
With a daily average of only 24,000 tickets sold in the first four days the organisers have been working around the clock seeking ways to attract a larger crowd in the remaining five days.
There are plans to give free tickets to police officers and to radio and television stations which will then offer them to listeners and viewers.

"Unfortunately the prospects for more tickets don't look very promising," a senior sports ministry official said. "The choice to hold the championships at the start of August was wrong and I expect heads to roll."
Ticket sales are also the only source of revenue for the organisers who are atready in the red. spending $36 million for the championships and expecting $7 million in return if all tickets were sold.
The limited interest prompted an attack by world athletics chief Primo Nebiolo who accused the organisers for not promoting the world championships sufficiently.
"There has maybe not been a great campaign of promotion," said Nebiolo, the president of the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) who is also backing Rome's rival bid for the 2004 Games.
"When we came around three weeks ago we understood that the promotion campaign was not being made. We tried to do it differently with the newspapers and TV."
The championships' general manager Vangelis Savramis countered that he had tried to persuade to IAAF to move the event at the end of August when people return from their summer leave.
"We asked the IAAF to move the championships to the end of the month when the stadium would be full. They didn't listen," he said.
Responding to a suggestion by Nebiolo to fill up the empty seats with soldiers such as at the 1995 world championships in Gothenburg, he replied: "Greek soldiers are for the country's defence."

Nebiolo is in a difficult position diplomatically at these championships since Athens and Rome are regarded as being the two favourites to win the IOC vote to host the Games.The success or failure of these championships could be an important factor.
Athens and Rome are bidding against Cape Town, Buenos Aires and Stockholm to host the 2004 Games. The decision will be taken in Lausanne on September 5. REUTER
